scenario.name: Elastic Security Labs — GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution
scenario.shortSubtitle: Elastic Security Labs · Crafted .MSC Console File, apds.dll Redirect & DotNetToJScript
scenario.overview: Imagine a brick city apartment building entrance with a glass vestibule, a wall of brass resident mailboxes, a doorman podium, and a glowing brass intercom buzzer panel. Standing outside the locked glass apartment vestibule, an uninvited caller presses a crafted sequence on the brass intercom buzzer pretending to be building maintenance. In this real-world scenario, the intruder steps up to the locked glass vestibule door blending in with everyday guests, then completes the covert maneuver at the brass intercom buzzer & elevator while the doorman visitor sign-in book records the anomaly. The doorman checks the visitor sign-in ledger against the intercom buzz history and realizes no maintenance visit was ever scheduled by management. In this scenario (T1218.014, Elastic Security Labs, GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: opening a Malicious .msc File Triggers, then using DotNetToJScript to Reconstruct a .NET, then spawning dllhost.exe. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Opening a Malicious .msc File Triggers, then Using DotNetToJScript to Reconstruct a .NET, then Spawning dllhost.exe, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 7 with the documented host and network chain.

specs.value: Elastic Security Labs — GrimResource (Joe Desimone & Samir Bousseaden)

details.description: Specially crafted XML .msc file containing an embedded APDS redirect URI and obfuscated VBScript/DotNetToJScript loader in its StringTable.
Trusted Windows Microsoft Management Console process that parses sccm-Updater.msc and evaluates the res://apds.dll/redirect.html DOM XSS payload.
Uses transformNode XSLT inside the apds.dll HTML context to invoke DotNetToJScript, deserializing a C# Cobalt Strike loader in memory.
Child dllhost.exe spawned by the .NET loader inside mmc.exe and injected with shellcode via indirect syscalls.

stages.title: MMC PARSES CRAFTED .MSC & LOADS APDS.DLL
stages.subtitle: res://apds.dll/redirect.html DOM XSS triggered inside mmc.exe
stages.description: Standing outside the locked glass apartment vestibule, an uninvited caller presses a crafted sequence on the brass intercom buzzer pretending to be building maintenance. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder steps up to the locked glass vestibule door blending in with everyday guests while everyday visitors and the building doorman go about their routine. The victim double-clicks a weaponized console file (invoice_audit.msc, an XML-based Windows Management Console file used to bypass email and browser blocks on .exe and .lnk files), which Windows automatically opens using the trusted system binary C:\Windows\System32\mmc.exe. Inside the .msc XML structure, the <StringTables> section points an embedded HTML panel to res://C:\Windows\System32\apds.dll/redirect.html?target=javascript:eval(...) (abusing an ancient HTML page baked inside Microsoft’s own apds.dll library that blindly passes its "target=" parameter into a browser redirect, CVE-2024-43572, immediately executing the attacker’s VBScript/JavaScript inside mmc.exe). C:\Windows\System32\apds.dll (the legacy Microsoft Help Center library shipped on every Windows installation) contains an embedded resource (redirect.html) that passes the target query parameter directly to document.location.replace() without sanitizing javascript: or vbscript: URI schemes, giving the .msc file full script execution inside mmc.exe’s privileged MSHTML Zone. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LOAD APDS.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK Signed MS DLL) from Node ① (#1 Malicious .MSC Delivery) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM).

stages.title: XSLT TRANSFORMNODE & DOTNETTOJSCRIPT CLR LOAD
stages.subtitle: Obfuscated VBScript deserializes C# loader into mmc.exe memory
stages.description: Fooled by the caller’s voice over the lobby intercom, the building doorman buzzes open the interior lobby door and reads out the hallway elevator code. Here in Step 2 inside the apartment lobby, the intruder uses borrowed access inside the apartment lobby to slip closer to the brass intercom buzzer & elevator without disturbing the resident locked mailboxes. Plain JScript cannot call low-level Windows memory APIs directly, so the script inside mmc.exe uses the DotNetToJScript technique: it creates a .NET BinaryFormatter COM object via ActiveX (new ActiveXObject("System.Runtime.Serialization.Formatters.Binary.BinaryFormatter")) and deserializes a Base64-encoded .NET assembly ("GrimLoader") directly in RAM (allowing the attacker to bridge from limited JScript into a full .NET program with complete Win32 API access inside mmc.exe, without ever dropping a .dll or .exe file onto the hard drive). Deserializing a crafted gadget chain via BinaryFormatter loads the .NET Common Language Runtime (clr.dll / mscoree.dll) into mmc.exe and invokes Assembly.Load(byte[]) in memory (giving the attacker full P/Invoke access to kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll from inside a Microsoft-signed console process). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DOTNETTOJSCRIPT / ⇠#2 ACK In-Memory CLR) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 mmc.exe (Management Console)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM).

stages.title: SACRIFICIAL DLLHOST.EXE SPAWN & INDIRECT SYSCALL INJECTION
stages.subtitle: mmc.exe spawns dllhost.exe and injects Cobalt Strike via DirtyCLR
stages.description: Slipping past the brass resident mailboxes straight into the elevator, the intruder gains access to private upper-floor corridors without ever owning an apartment key. In this final step inside the apartment lobby, the intruder completes the covert maneuver at the brass intercom buzzer & elevator while the doorman visitor sign-in book records the anomaly until the doorman visitor sign-in book catches the mismatch. If the victim notices an empty console window and clicks "X" to close mmc.exe, any malware running inside mmc.exe would die immediately. To survive, the in-memory .NET loader spawns a hidden background C:\Windows\System32\dllhost.exe process (COM Surrogate, a legitimate Windows background host that runs without a visible taskbar window), maps a shared Read-Write-Execute memory section via NtCreateSection / NtMapViewOfSection ("RwSection" technique documented by Elastic Security Labs, avoiding suspicious VirtualAllocEx calls), and injects the Cobalt Strike C2 beacon into dllhost.exe. Migrating execution from the interactive mmc.exe process into a headless dllhost.exe process via shared section mapping (RwSection) or Asynchronous Procedure Call (NtQueueApcThread) ensures the C2 beacon stays alive in the background long after the victim closes the .msc window. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 & 8 exchange from mmc.exe (Management Console) to apds.dll & DotNetToJScript, apds.dll & DotNetToJScript responds with ACK PID 6088 (confirming that the INJECT DLLHOST.EXE request succeeded on apds.dll & DotNetToJScript and completing the final execution objective of Elastic Security Labs, GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ INJECT DLLHOST.EXE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6088) from Node ③ (#3 mmc.exe (Management Console)) to Node ④ (#4 apds.dll & DotNetToJScript), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM).

detectionRule.title: Elastic Security Labs — GrimResource MMC Loading apds.dll (Sysmon EID 7)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: GrimResource Exploitation via MMC Loading apds.dll
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\mmc.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\apds.dll'
  condition: selection
level: high
detectionRule.mitigation: Block untrusted .msc files from email/web gateways and monitor mmc.exe loading apds.dll alongside jscript.dll or vbscript.dll.

detectionRule.title: Elastic Security Labs YARA — Windows.Trojan.GrimResource (.MSC File)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule Windows_Trojan_GrimResource_MSC {
  meta:
    author = "Elastic Security Labs"
    description = "Detects MSC files abusing apds.dll redirect.html (GrimResource)"
  strings:
    $msc = "<MMC_ConsoleFile" ascii wide nocase
    $apds = "apds.dll/redirect.html" ascii wide nocase
    $js = "javascript:" ascii wide nocase
  condition:
    $msc and $apds and $js
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Scan inbound .msc attachments for references to apds.dll/redirect.html and embedded ActiveX/XSLT script blocks.

detectionRule.title: Suspicious Bare dllhost.exe Spawned by mmc.exe (GrimResource Injection)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: GrimResource MMC Spawning Sacrificial dllhost.exe
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\mmc.exe'
    Image|endswith: '\dllhost.exe'
  filter_legit_com:
    CommandLine|contains: '/Processid:'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit_com
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Alert on any dllhost.exe process spawned without /Processid:{GUID} command-line arguments, especially when parented by mmc.exe.
